paths.title: Go Deeper: Senior Product Management with a Growth/Experimentation Specialty
paths.summary: Build on your current APM role by moving toward senior and eventually lead product roles focused on activation, retention, and growth experimentation. This path leverages the analytical-storytelling combination you've been sharpening since college.
paths.whyItFits: Your thesis on how people share news online, the Google Analytics certification, and your work lifting activation by 18% at Brightpath Health all show a consistent thread of using data to drive product decisions. The Product management certificate and habit tracker project also show you can take an idea from discovery to shipped experiments.
blindSpots: Growth-focused PM roles at larger companies often require more rigorous statistical rigor (e.g., proper A/B test power calculations) than a wellness app onboarding flow may have demanded.
Moving up the ladder usually means less hands-on experimentation and more stakeholder management and roadmap prioritization across competing teams.
Specializing narrowly in growth/activation could pigeonhole you if you later want to move into general management or a different product domain.
The jump from APM to senior PM often requires a portfolio of shipped, measurable wins beyond one activation lift, and you may need 1-2 more clear wins first.

skillGaps.whereYouAre: You ran five small experiments at Brightpath and did A/B testing at Fernway, but there's no evidence yet of formal experiment design (sample size, significance testing) beyond practical iteration.
skillGaps.nextStep: Take a short applied course or read a practical guide on A/B testing statistics and apply the concepts to your next Brightpath experiment.

skillGaps.whereYouAre: Your product certificate covered roadmapping and you've done prioritisation on the habit tracker, but there's no evidence of using structured frameworks (RICE, ICE, etc.) at scale.
skillGaps.nextStep: Practice applying a named prioritization framework to your current backlog at Brightpath and present the reasoning to your manager.

skillGaps.whereYouAre: You've done cross-team work shipping the onboarding redesign, but leading larger, multi-team initiatives isn't yet demonstrated.
skillGaps.nextStep: Volunteer to lead a slightly larger initiative spanning more than one team at Brightpath, even informally.

skillGaps.whereYouAre: No evidence in your story yet of building revenue models or business cases tied to product decisions.
skillGaps.nextStep: Learn basic unit economics and try building a simple model estimating the revenue impact of one of your onboarding experiments.

firstSteps.action: Find a mentor or peer group of senior PMs in growth-focused roles.
firstSteps.howToFind: Search for 'product growth Slack community' or 'growth PM meetup' plus your city name.

firstSteps.action: Identify 2-3 senior product manager job postings to reverse-engineer the skill gap.
firstSteps.howToFind: Search job boards using the phrase 'senior product manager growth activation' to see common requirements.

firstSteps.action: Read foundational material on experimentation design.
firstSteps.howToFind: Search for 'A/B testing statistics for product managers guide' on a reputable analytics or product blog.

firstSteps.action: Ask your manager at Brightpath for a stretch project tied to retention, not just activation.
firstSteps.howToFind: This is internal — prepare a one-page proposal referencing your activation results as leverage.

paths.confidenceNote: This is a natural extension of your demonstrated trajectory, but I can't verify current hiring demand or compensation for growth PM roles in your specific market.

paths.title: Pivot: People-Centered Coaching and Career Development
paths.summary: Shift from building products to building people, moving into a formal coaching, learning & development, or career-services role. This path centers the mentoring and teaching instincts you've clearly enjoyed cultivating.
paths.whyItFits: You've mentored 14 career changers with three landing product roles, and your reflection that 'explaining my own path clearly taught me what I still need to learn' suggests real energy here. Your people management experience at Fernway and your own well-documented career transition (via the product certificate) give you credible material to teach from.
blindSpots: Coaching and L&D roles often pay less than product management, at least initially, and you'd be stepping away from a growth trajectory you've already invested years building.
Volunteer mentoring success (3 of 14 placed) is a small sample; formal coaching roles may require measurable outcomes at a larger scale and more accountability.
This path may require additional credentialing (coaching certification) depending on the setting, which is a real time and money cost.
You may miss the built-something-tangible satisfaction you got from the habit tracker and onboarding redesign if the role becomes purely advisory.

skillGaps.whereYouAre: You run intake calls and review portfolios informally for mentees, but there's no evidence of formal coaching frameworks or certifications.
skillGaps.nextStep: Look into a recognized coaching methodology or certification program and see if the format fits your goals.

skillGaps.whereYouAre: No evidence in your story yet of designing structured multi-week learning programs, only one-to-one mentoring.
skillGaps.nextStep: Try designing a small structured cohort-based program for your meetup mentees instead of one-off calls.

skillGaps.whereYouAre: You track placement outcomes informally (3 of 14), but haven't built formal measurement systems.
skillGaps.nextStep: Borrow your product instincts: define clear success metrics and a simple dashboard for your mentoring outcomes, similar to your Fernway reporting work.

skillGaps.whereYouAre: Your podcast interviewing skills and one-to-one mentoring show comfort with conversation, but group facilitation isn't yet evidenced.
skillGaps.nextStep: Offer to run a group workshop session at your meetup instead of only 1:1 calls, to build this muscle.

firstSteps.action: Talk to people currently working in corporate L&D, coaching, or career services to understand day-to-day reality and pay.
firstSteps.howToFind: Search 'informational interview career coach' or 'L&D manager' on a professional networking site and request a short call.

firstSteps.action: Explore whether your current meetup mentoring could formalize into a paid or structured offering.
firstSteps.howToFind: Search 'how to start a career coaching side practice' for practical starting guides.

firstSteps.action: Investigate coaching certification options to see fit and cost.
firstSteps.howToFind: Search 'ICF accredited coaching certification programs' to compare options.

firstSteps.action: Pilot a small paid coaching cohort using your product-launch instincts.
firstSteps.howToFind: This is something you can design yourself, using your habit-tracker prototyping approach: sketch the offer, test with a few willing mentees.

paths.confidenceNote: Your mentoring impact is real but small-scale, and I have no way to verify job availability, pay, or demand for coaching/L&D roles in your area.

paths.title: Blend: Founder or Early Product Lead for a Community/Health-Adjacent Startup
paths.summary: Combine your product management experience, entrepreneurial track record (tote bag shop, habit tracker), and interest in health/wellness (via Brightpath) to build or join an early-stage startup as a founding product person. This path merges the maker energy of your side projects with your current domain expertise.
paths.whyItFits: You've already run two independent ventures (the tote bag shop with real revenue and repeat customers, and the habit tracker with 300 sign-ups), and you're currently embedded in wellness product work at Brightpath Health with a proven activation win. Your discipline shown in half-marathon training and your comfort with ambiguity from these side projects suggest founder resilience.
blindSpots: Founding or joining an early-stage startup means giving up the relative stability of your current role and likely a pay cut or equity-heavy compensation you can't easily evaluate without deeper research.
Your side projects, while successful for their scale (hundreds of users, a few thousand dollars revenue), are far from proof you can raise funding or run a company with employees.
Health-adjacent startups often carry regulatory complexity (privacy, clinical claims) that your current onboarding-focused role may not have exposed you to.
Being a solo or co-founder demands skills like fundraising, legal structuring, and hiring that aren't yet reflected anywhere in your timeline.

skillGaps.whereYouAre: No evidence in your story yet of raising capital or pitching investors; your ventures were self-funded and bootstrapped.
skillGaps.nextStep: Attend a startup pitch event or accelerator info session to learn the basics of how fundraising conversations work.

skillGaps.skill: Technical/engineering collaboration at a deeper level
skillGaps.whereYouAre: You worked with engineering on the onboarding redesign and used no-code tools for the habit tracker, but haven't built or managed a technical product from scratch with a dedicated engineering team.
skillGaps.nextStep: Consider partnering with or shadowing a technical co-founder type, or take a light technical fluency course to speak the language more fluently.

skillGaps.whereYouAre: You work at a wellness app but there's no evidence of hands-on experience with health data regulations or clinical claims.
skillGaps.nextStep: Research basic health-tech compliance basics (e.g., data privacy standards relevant to health apps) relevant to your interest area.

skillGaps.whereYouAre: You managed a team of three at Fernway, but building a founding team from zero is different and untested.
skillGaps.nextStep: Talk to early-stage founders about how they made their first few hires to understand the process before attempting it yourself.

firstSteps.action: Talk to founders of small health/wellness startups about their early days, funding, and regrets.
firstSteps.howToFind: Search 'health tech startup founder informational interview' or attend a local startup demo night — search 'startup demo day' plus your city.

firstSteps.action: Test a new, smaller side project idea in the health/wellness space using your no-code and prototyping skills.
firstSteps.howToFind: This is self-directed: apply the same paper-sketch-then-no-code approach you used for the habit tracker to a new wellness-adjacent idea.

firstSteps.action: Explore part-time or advisory involvement with an early-stage startup before committing fully.
firstSteps.howToFind: Search 'early stage startup advisor product' on a startup job board or networking platform.

firstSteps.action: Learn fundraising basics through free resources before considering founding anything.
firstSteps.howToFind: Search 'startup fundraising basics for first-time founders guide'.

paths.confidenceNote: This path draws on real entrepreneurial signals in your history, but startup outcomes are highly uncertain and I have no way to assess current market conditions, funding climate, or your personal risk tolerance for this leap.

caveat: These three paths are starting points for exploration and conversation, not predictions about what will or should happen in your career.
